question: Which three annotations does `@SpringBootApplication` combine?
options: `@Controller`, `@Service` and `@Repository`
`@Bean`, `@Autowired` and `@Qualifier`
`@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration` and `@ComponentScan`
`@Entity`, `@Table` and `@Id`
explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` marks the class as a configuration class, turns on auto-configuration based on the libraries on the classpath, and scans the class's package and its sub-packages for components. That is why the main class normally sits in the root package.

question: Which style of dependency injection does the Spring team recommend for required dependencies?
options: Constructor injection, as shown, because dependencies can be `final` and the class is easy to test.
Field injection with `@Autowired`, because it needs less code.
Creating the dependency with `new` inside the class.
Looking the bean up from a static `ApplicationContext` holder.
explanation: With constructor injection the object cannot exist without its dependencies, the fields can be `final`, and a test can pass a mock straight to the constructor. A class with a single constructor does not even need `@Autowired`.

question: What is the difference between `@Controller` and `@RestController` in Spring?
options: `@RestController` can only handle GET requests.
`@Controller` is for Spring Boot and `@RestController` is for Spring MVC.
`@RestController` creates a new instance for every request.
`@RestController` adds `@ResponseBody`, so return values are written to the response body (usually as JSON) instead of being treated as view names.
explanation: `@RestController` is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`. A method in a plain `@Controller` that returns `"home"` renders the view called home; in a `@RestController` the same return value is sent as the response body, and objects are converted to JSON by Jackson.

question: What is the default scope of a Spring bean, and what does it imply?
options: `prototype`: a new instance is created every time the bean is injected.
`singleton`: one shared instance per application context, so it should not keep per-request state in fields.
`request`: one instance per HTTP request.
`session`: one instance per logged-in user.
explanation: Beans are singletons unless declared otherwise. The same service or controller object handles all requests on many threads at once, so mutable fields holding data of one request are a concurrency bug.

question: In this Spring service, `importAll()` is called from a controller. Why does `saveOne()` not run in its own new transaction?
options: `REQUIRES_NEW` is only allowed on private methods.
`@Transactional` works only on repository interfaces.
The call is made on `this`, so it bypasses the Spring proxy that applies `@Transactional`.
Transactions cannot be started inside a loop.
explanation: Spring applies `@Transactional` through a proxy that wraps the bean. Only calls that come in through the proxy are intercepted. A call from one method to another in the same object goes straight to `this`, so the annotation on `saveOne()` is ignored. The usual fix is to move `saveOne()` to another bean.

question: By default, for which exceptions does a Spring `@Transactional` method roll back the transaction?
options: Unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException` and `Error`), but not checked exceptions.
Every exception, checked or unchecked.
Only `SQLException`.
None; rollback must always be called manually.
explanation: The default rule rolls back on `RuntimeException` and `Error` and commits when a checked exception is thrown. To roll back on a checked exception as well, declare it: `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`.

question: A Spring Boot project has `application.properties` and `application-prod.properties`. The app starts with `spring.profiles.active=prod`. Which values are used?
options: Only `application-prod.properties`; the base file is ignored.
Only `application.properties`; profile files are for tests.
The app fails to start because two files define properties.
Both are loaded, and values in `application-prod.properties` override the same keys in `application.properties`.
explanation: The base file holds the common settings and each profile file holds only what differs. When a profile is active its file is loaded on top, so its keys win. This is how one build runs with different database URLs in development and production.

question: What does Spring Data JPA do with this repository method that has no implementation?
options: It fails to compile because interface methods need a body.
It derives the query from the method name: users whose `email` matches and whose `active` is true.
It returns every user and filters the list in memory.
It calls a stored procedure named `findByEmailAndActiveTrue`.
explanation: Spring Data parses the method name into a query (`findBy` + property + keyword) and generates the implementation at startup. If a property in the name does not exist on the entity, the application fails to start, which catches typos early. Complex queries use `@Query` instead.

question: An endpoint loads 100 `Order` entities and then reads `order.getCustomer().getName()` for each one. The log shows 101 SQL queries. What is this problem and a standard fix?
options: A deadlock; fix it by adding `synchronized` to the method.
A connection leak; fix it by increasing the connection pool size.
The N+1 select problem; load the association in the same query with `JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph`.
A missing index; fix it by adding `@Index` on the `id` column.
explanation: One query loads the orders, then each lazy `customer` triggers its own query: 1 + N. A fetch join (`select o from Order o join fetch o.customer`) or an `@EntityGraph` loads both in one round trip. Switching the mapping to `EAGER` everywhere is not a real fix, because it loads the data even when it is not needed.

question: For the request `GET /products/42?currency=OMR`, how does this Spring method receive `42` and `OMR`?
codeSnippet:
@GetMapping("/products/{id}")
public Product get(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestParam String currency) { /* ... */ }
options: `@PathVariable` reads `42` from the URL path and `@RequestParam` reads `OMR` from the query string.
`@PathVariable` reads `OMR` from the query string and `@RequestParam` reads `42` from the path.
Both values are read from the request body.
Both values are read from HTTP headers.
explanation: `@PathVariable` binds a `{placeholder}` segment of the path, which identifies the resource. `@RequestParam` binds a query string parameter (after the `?`), which is normally used for options such as filters, sorting and paging.

question: What do you get by adding the single dependency `spring-boot-starter-web` to a project?
options: Only the Spring annotations; a web server must be installed separately.
A React front end generated from your controllers.
A database and an ORM configured for production.
Spring MVC, JSON support through Jackson and an embedded Tomcat server, with compatible versions chosen for you.
explanation: A starter is a dependency that pulls in a tested set of libraries for one purpose. With the web starter the application runs as a plain JAR with `java -jar`, because Tomcat is embedded, and auto-configuration wires MVC and JSON conversion without XML.

question: How do you return the same JSON error format from every controller in a Spring Boot API when a `NotFoundException` is thrown?
options: Wrap the body of every controller method in `try/catch`.
Write one class annotated with `@RestControllerAdvice` that has an `@ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)` method.
Set `server.error.format=json` in `application.properties`.
Throw the exception from a `static` block.
explanation: `@RestControllerAdvice` applies to all controllers. Its `@ExceptionHandler` methods turn an exception into a response (status code and body) in one place, so controllers stay free of repeated error handling.

question: What does Spring Boot Actuator add to an application?
options: A visual drag-and-drop editor for controllers.
Automatic translation of the API into other languages.
Production endpoints such as `/actuator/health` and metrics for monitoring the running application.
A replacement for the Java garbage collector.
explanation: Actuator exposes operational information over HTTP or JMX: health, metrics, environment, loggers and more. Load balancers and Kubernetes probes commonly call `/actuator/health`. Only a few endpoints are exposed over HTTP by default, and sensitive ones should be secured.

question: A client posts `{"email": ""}` to this Spring Boot endpoint. What happens?
options: Validation fails before the method body runs and the client gets `400 Bad Request`.
The method runs with `email` set to `null`.
The application shuts down with a validation error.
The client gets `200 OK` and the error is only logged.
explanation: `@Valid` makes Spring run Bean Validation on the deserialized body. A violation throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which Spring maps to a 400 response, so the method never sees invalid input. This needs `spring-boot-starter-validation` on the classpath.

question: Two classes annotated with `@Component` implement the interface `Notifier`. What happens when Spring builds this service, and how is it fixed?
options: Spring injects the implementation whose class name comes first alphabetically.
Spring injects both, one after the other.
Spring injects `null` and the service fails on first use.
Startup fails with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`; mark one bean `@Primary` or choose one with `@Qualifier`.
explanation: Injection by type needs exactly one candidate. With two, Spring refuses to guess and the context fails to start. `@Primary` sets a default, `@Qualifier("name")` picks one at the injection point, and injecting `List<Notifier>` receives all of them.
